newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat gives condolences, ready to meet Israeli PM.
newsitem.headline: Arafat gives condolences, ready to meet Israeli PM.

text.p: Yasser Arafat, in remarks broadcast on Friday, expressed sorrow at the killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a Jordanian soldier and said the most important thing now was to push peace forward.

Asked by Israel Radio if he would meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the Palestinian president said in English: "I have no objection. The most important thing (is) how to push forward the peace process".

"I am very sorry at what had happened and I contacted his excellency the president and his excellency the prime minister and offered my condolences by the name of the Palestinian people," Arafat said, confirming reports he had telephoned Israel's President Ezer Weizman and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Arafat was speaking late on Thursday.
The telephone call to the prime minister was the first contact between the two leaders since Arafat angrily rejected last week a planned Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank.

Arafat aide Marwan Kanafani told Reuters on Thursday: "The president is willing to meet Netanyahu if the meeting is to discuss the latest Israeli measures, including the settlement in (Arab East Jerusalem) and (West Bank) redeployment."

Israel buried the seven girls, aged 12 to 13, on Thursday night. A Jordanian soldier shot them dead earlier in the day while they were on a school trip to a border site nicknamed "The Island of Peace".
Netanyahu's spokesman reported Arafat's phone call. He quoted Netanyahu as telling Arafat: "There can be differences of opinion but there is no place for all the talk about violence."

Palestinian officials and Jordan's King Hussein had warned of the danger of bloodshed if Israel went ahead with plans to build 6,500 more homes for Jews on land captured in 1967 between East Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
Netanyahu, delivering the main eulogy at the funeral of four of the girls late on Thursday, said the incident only reaffirmed Israel's commitment to tighten its hold on all of Jerusalem.

"If anyone thinks the murder of little girls will bring this people to its knees...or that we will relinquish our birthright, holy land and eternal capital, he does not know the strength that exists in each person standing here around me today and in the entire nation," he said.

Israel-PLO relations plunged further when the Israeli government announced last week that a West Bank pullback, one of three due to be completed by mid-1998, would be only a third of the size demanded by the PLO.

Israel said on Thursday senior Palestine Liberation Organisation official Mahmoud Abbas, also known as Abu Mazen, phoned Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy to express condolences over the killings on the Jordanian border.

Abu Mazen, architect of the 1993 Israel-PLO self-rule deal and chief Palestinian negotiator with Israel, tendered his resignation to Arafat in protest at Israel's moves on settlement and redeployment. Arafat has yet to decide whether to accept it.
